extracted.intended_audience: practitioners admitted or seeking to practice before the USPTO (patent attorneys and agents); Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff; Administrative Law Judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedures, and sanctioning criteria applied in USPTO disciplinary proceedings against patent practitioners (rules on service/default, prohibited conduct, certification of papers, and factors for imposing sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer / default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent is properly served and does not file an answer within the prescribed period, the respondent is deemed to have admitted the factual allegations and the OED Director may move for entry of default judgment. The decision treats admitted allegations as established facts for purposes of the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by publication requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When service by mail cannot be obtained, the OED Director may serve a respondent by notice via publication in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks; when served this way, respondent must file an answer within thirty days of the second publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to publication service, an attempt at service by first-class certified mail with return receipt is typically made; publication dates are the triggering dates for computing the 30-day answer deadline (e.g., second publication date + 30 days = answer due).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of papers — no improper purpose (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting a paper to the Office, the practitioner certifies that to the best of the practitioner's knowledge, information, and belief the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose, such as harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of § 11.18 (presenting papers for an improper purpose) are misconduct and subject to sanctions, including referral to OED. Examples: filings that contain only verbal abuse and no substantive amendments may be stricken and may support disciplinary charges under § 11.18(b)(2)(i) and (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'disreputable conduct' encompasses unprofessional conduct 'violative of the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor.' Conduct that brings the profession into disrepute or lessens public confidence in the profession falls within this prohibition. The Court looks to case law and professional norms to evaluate whether conduct is disreputable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney's conduct is prejudicial when it negatively impacts the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession. Courts have sanctioned speech likely to 'obstruct or prejudice the administration of justice.' Abusive, harassing communications that undermine public confidence in the Office/examiners fall within this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on undignified or discourteous conduct before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 10.89(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: In appearing in a professional capacity before a tribunal, a practitioner shall not engage in undignified or discourteous conduct before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is intended to prohibit undignified, discourteous, or disrespectful conduct or remarks; it is a call to discretion and civility, not to silence legitimate criticism. The decision consults ordinary dictionary meanings (discourteous = rude or impolite; undignified = not serious or formal) to assess submissions. Official submissions are 'official' and practitioners must consider their words carefully; ad hominem attacks, slurs, and demeaning language are examples of prohibited conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all: conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subsection is a residual provision; if alleged conduct falls under earlier subsections (b)(1)-(b)(5), it cannot separately be charged under (b)(6). The Director must identify conduct that does not already fall within the other listed prohibitions to sustain a (b)(6) charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider four factors: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court uses these factors, together with reference to ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and relevant authority, to determine the nature and severity of disciplinary sanctions (e.g., suspension length). Each factor is evaluated on the record: duties breached (client interests, public confidence, respect for the Office), mental state (intentionality), injury (actual vs. potential reputational or client harm), and aggravators/mitigators (multiple offenses, remorse, disciplinary history, motive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of aggravating and mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include multiple offenses, lack of acceptance of responsibility, and lack of remorse; mitigating factors may include long-standing admission to the bar with no prior disciplinary record and absence of dishonest or selfish motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of multiple separate improper filings and a demonstrated lack of remorse or recognition of misconduct support harsher sanctions. Conversely, substantial practice tenure without prior discipline and no evidence of dishonest/selfish motivation may mitigate the sanction. The Court weighs these in applying § 11.54(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: When speech may be sanctioned: likelihood to obstruct or prejudice administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney's speech may be sanctioned if it is highly likely to obstruct or prejudice the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law indicates that progressively abusive language, threats, or demeanor that are likely to obstruct or prejudice the judicial process or the public's confidence in it can support disciplinary measures. The Court applies this principle to abusive filings widely disseminated (e.g., posted online), which can cause reputational harm to examiners and the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of filings that are inappropriate papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may strike from the record papers determined to be inappropriate under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(c)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that lack legitimate purpose (e.g., two-page 'remarks' consisting entirely of insults with no amendments) can be stricken as inappropriate papers and serve as the basis for discipline under the certification rule. Public dissemination of such filings increases potential injury and sanction severity.
